abstract: Natural history collections contain vast amounts of undocumented biodiversity, yet degraded DNA has long limited their integration into modern barcode reference systems. Here, we present a cost-effective Oxford Nanopore Technologies (ONT)-based workflow for recovering COI barcodes from historical spider museum specimens, using the taxonomically challenging jumping spider genus Cytaea as a model system. We developed a mini-barcoding approach based on six short overlapping COI fragments (~130 bp), amplified in two multiplex PCR reactions and sequenced on ONT Flongle flow cells. The workflow was applied to 288 museum specimens ranging from 13 to 141 years old, preserved primarily in 75% ethanol under standard museum conditions. COI data were recovered from 284 of 288 specimens (98.6%). Reconstructed sequences ranged from 115 to 663 bp, and 260 of the 284 sequences (91.5%) contained at least 300 bp of resolved sequence. Amplification success differed strongly among primer pairs (31.6-98.3%), highlighting the importance of marker optimization for degraded DNA. Although older specimens generally yielded shorter sequences, informative barcode data were recovered even from century-old material. The combined ONT and Sanger dataset substantially expanded the documented barcode diversity of Cytaea, revealing 54 BINs, including 53 newly added to BOLD. Because fragmented mini-barcodes complicate standard clustering approaches, we placed short sequences onto a reference backbone constructed from full-length COI barcodes. This enabled their assignment to major lineages, although placement confidence varied among specimens. Our results demonstrate that historical museum specimens can be efficiently transformed into usable barcode resources using a simple, scalable, and affordable ONT-based workflow. This approach provides a practical bridge between legacy museum collections and modern DNA-based taxonomy, enabling degraded historical material to be incorporated into global biodiversity reference systems.
